question: For a positive integer $p$, define the positive integer $n$ to be $p$-safe if $n$ differs in absolute value by more than $2$ from all multiples of $p$. For example, the set of $10$-safe numbers is $\{ 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 23, \ldots\}$. Find the number of positive integers less than or equal to $10,000$ which are simultaneously $7$-safe, $11$-safe, and $13$-safe.
solution:
If \(r\) is the remainder of \(n\) modulo \(p\), safety requires both \(r>2\) and \(p-r>2\). Thus the allowed remainders are 3 through \(p-3\), giving \(p-5\) choices. For 7, 11, and 13 there are respectively 2, 6, and 8 choices.
Since the moduli are pairwise coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem gives exactly one residue modulo \(7\cdot11\cdot13=1001\) for each allowed triple. Thus every block of 1001 consecutive integers contains \(2\cdot6\cdot8=96\) simultaneously safe numbers. From 1 through 10,010 there are ten blocks, giving 960.
To stop at 10,000, remove the numbers \(10010-k\) for \(0\le k\le9\). Since 10,010 is a multiple of all three moduli, their distances from the nearest multiples are the same as for \(k\). Only \(k=3,4\) are 7-safe in this range, and both are also 11-safe and 13-safe. Subtracting these two gives \(960-2=958\).
Final answer: 958
